OIL PIPELINEs GEOPOLITICS: Saudi Arabia has announced plans today to expand its key East-West pipeline (bypassing the Strait of Hormuz), which has a nominal capacity of 7m b/d (although currently is running probably at around 6m b/d after an attack destroyed a pumping station in September). 

In the next 7-8 weeks, Saudi Aramco would be able to boost capacity by 1.2m b/d using an existing natural gas pipe, making changes to ship crude. Riyadh didn't disclose further details, other than the line would need to revert to nat gas by May as the kingdom needs it to feed power stations during the summer months. 

[My hypothesis is this could be the old 48-inches, ~1,500-km long IPSA (Iraqi Pipeline in Saudi Arabia) built in the 1980s which runs largely parallel to the East-West pipeline from pumping station #3 all the way to near Yanbu. The pipeline was seized by the Saudis after Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in Aug 1990 and later it was repurposed for use in the country's Master Gas System]

More long-term, Saudi officials said they plan to boost shipping capacity of the East-West pipeline to ~10m b/d in the next 2-3 years, mostly improving pumping capacity (rather than building another pipe).

U.S. FORWARD OIL prices are climbing gradually and sending a slightly stronger signal to increase production. Twelve-month forward WTI futures have climbed to an average of almost $78 per barrel so far in October, the highest for more than two years, and up from just $58 in December 2025. The futures contract is trading almost exactly in line with the long-term average since 2010 or 2000 after adjusting for inflation. Crucially, it is trading above the $65-70 per barrel producers have said they need to drill new wells profitably in the Permian Basin. Futures prices are close to a level that should support production at existing levels and possibly spur some very small growth:

As expected, Trump's diesel deal with Putin has barely moved the needle, given the relatively small volumes involved. Both US ULSD and European gasoil cracks remain exceptionally elevated, highlighting the persistent shortage of refined products. While additional Russian supply may provide some marginal relief, it does little to offset the much larger disruption to Middle East exports and the loss of regional refining capacity. The widening divergence between diesel and gasoline cracks on both sides of the Atlantic underscores that the current supply crisis remains overwhelmingly concentrated in middle distillates, which include jet and maritime fuels, and heating oil.
